title: Distributed job scheduler
summary: Durable schedules, leases, retries and exactly-once effects.
prompt: Design a scheduler that runs millions of jobs: one-off delayed jobs and recurring cron-style jobs submitted by other teams, executed by a pool of workers, with retries and visibility into each run.

requirements: Functional: create, update and cancel jobs (one-off at a time, or a cron expression), run them on workers, retry failures, show run history.
Non-functional: jobs start within seconds of their due time, no scheduled run is lost, at most one active execution per run, scales to millions of jobs.
estimation: 10M scheduled jobs, 100M runs a day ≈ 1,150 runs/s average, with spikes at the top of each hour when many cron jobs align.
Run history ~500 bytes × 100M a day ≈ 50 GB a day; keep 30 days hot.
api: POST /jobs {schedule, target, payload, timeout, retryPolicy, idempotencyKey} → {jobId}.
DELETE /jobs/{id}; GET /jobs/{id}/runs?cursor= → run states and logs.
Worker protocol: lease(n) → runs; heartbeat(runId); complete(runId, result).
data: jobs(id, owner, schedule, next_run_at, target, payload, enabled, version), indexed on next_run_at and sharded by job ID.
runs(run_id, job_id, scheduled_for, attempt, status, lease_owner, lease_expires_at), unique on (job_id, scheduled_for).
design: Scheduler shards scan their partition for due jobs, create a run row (the unique key prevents duplicates), advance next_run_at, and enqueue the run.
Workers lease runs with a timeout and heartbeat; if a worker dies, the lease expires and another worker takes the run.
On failure, retries are rescheduled with exponential backoff and jitter; after max attempts the run is marked failed and the owner alerted.
deepDives: At-least-once execution is the realistic guarantee: a worker can finish the side effect then crash before reporting. Pass a run ID so targets can be idempotent, which gives exactly-once effects.
Fencing: each lease carries an increasing token; targets or storage reject writes from an older token, so a paused “zombie” worker cannot overwrite a newer attempt.
Hot minutes: add a small deterministic jitter to cron jobs that allow it, and pre-load due jobs a few seconds early into a time-bucketed queue.
bottlenecks: Scanning a huge next_run_at index: partition by shard and by time bucket, and claim shards via leader leases.
Noisy tenants: per-tenant concurrency limits and fair queues.
Long-running jobs: heartbeats extend leases; set a hard timeout.
tradeoffs: Exactly-once execution is not achievable across failures; at-least-once plus idempotent targets is the practical answer.
Polling the database is simple but adds latency and load; a time-wheel or delay queue is faster but harder to make durable.
Strict start-time accuracy vs smoothing spikes with jitter.

rubric.text: Stored schedules durably with an index on next run time.
Prevented duplicate runs with a unique run key.
Used leases with heartbeats and expiry for worker failures.
Retried with backoff and capped attempts, with alerting.
Stated at-least-once execution and required idempotent targets.
Used fencing tokens against zombie workers.
Smoothed hot-minute spikes and isolated noisy tenants.
